th-1016-1.text:
Nerves before a fight don't mean you're not ready.

They mean your body knows it matters.

The fighters who look calm aren't fearless. They just stopped reading fear as a stop sign.

th-1016-2.text:
Honest question for the fighters here.

What's the round you dread most in training?

First round cold, the middle grind, or the last one when everything's gone?

th-1016-3.text:
No coach? Film every session.

You can't fix what you can't see. Watch it the same day, pick one thing, fix only that this week.

One fix a week is 52 fixes a year.

th-1017-1.text:
Discipline isn't motivation.

It's kept promises.

Pick one thing you do every single day. Keep it for 30 days. That's where the mindset actually comes from.

th-1017-2.text:
Which one is you?

1. You train when no fight is booked
2. You keep going after getting dropped in sparring
3. You've never needed a crowd to show up

Drop the number.

th-1017-3.text:
The sparring session you lose to someone better is worth more than ten you win.

Getting picked apart shows you every hole at once.

Watch it back the same night. Every mistake is right there.

th-1018-1.text:
You're mentally tougher than you think if you've lost and come back the next day.

Not the next week. The next day.

That's the whole test.

th-1018-2.text:
What do you say in your head when you get hit clean?

One word beats a speech. Something like: reset.

What's yours?

th-1018-3.text: How to stay calm in a fight when you don't have years of experience. A thread.

th-1019-1.text:
A bad session ruining your whole day isn't weakness.

It means you care more than most people in the gym.

Just don't let it ruin tomorrow's session too.

th-1019-2.text:
Rest days.

Do they feel like recovery or like punishment?

Be honest.

th-1019-3.text:
You don't need weights to hit harder.

Turn the back foot. Relax until impact. Exhale sharp on every shot.

Power starts on the floor. No pivot, no punch.

th-1020-1.text:
The hardest punch isn't the strongest one.

It's the one they walk into.

Timing beats strength every time.

th-1020-2.text:
Training alone this week?

What's your go-to solo session?

Shadowboxing, bag rounds, footwork, or tape study?

th-1020-3.text:
No partner? Give every bag round a rule.

Only counters this round. Only body shots the next.

You build reactions, not just punches.

th-1021-1.text:
Fear before a fight isn't the problem.

Feel it. Name it. Walk out anyway.

That's the entire skill.

th-1021-2.text:
Started combat sports late?

How old were you when you walked into your first gym?

Curious how many of you are out there.

th-1021-3.text:
When training suddenly feels harder, most people think they're getting worse.

Usually it's the opposite.

You're starting to notice mistakes you couldn't see before. That's what leveling up feels like from the inside.

th-1022-1.text:
Stop caring how it looks.

Start caring if it works.

That switch is when you actually start getting good.

th-1022-2.text:
Which one is you?

1. Training feels harder, not easier
2. The guys who used to beat you are struggling now
3. Sparring feels slower than it used to

Drop the number.

th-1022-3.text:
Started late? Ask more questions than anyone in the gym.

One question a session to the best person there.

Most will help. Nobody's ever annoyed by someone who wants to learn.

th-1023-1.text:
Hard sparring every week makes most beginners worse, not tougher.

You learn to survive, not to fight. Light rounds with one rule teach more than a war you just get through.

th-1023-2.text:
Cardio, hands or head: which one goes first for you in round three?

Pick one. Then say what you do when it goes.

th-1023-3.text:
I had a ruptured appendix the day before a fight.

That's the closest I've come to quitting. What kept me in it wasn't a plan. It was "I can't give up."

Not smart advice. Just the honest answer.

th-1024-1.text:
Shadowboxing without a target is cardio with your hands up.

Pick an opponent. Give him a lefty stance and a habit of dropping his right. Then fight him for three rounds.

th-1024-2.text:
What did your first coach get wrong?

Or what did they get right that you only understood a year later?

th-1025-1.text:
Comparing yourself to the guy a year ahead is how people quit.

He's already made a year of mistakes you haven't. Compare yourself to you in March.

th-1025-2.text:
What do you still do from month one, even though you know it's wrong?

Common one: dropping the back hand after the jab.

th-1025-3.text: Your jab feels weak? Check these five things before you blame your arm.

th-1026-1.text:
I tore a knee ligament in a street fight.

I took a guy down like a BJJ guy, on pavement. The mat has rules. Pavement doesn't. Training for a sport and training for the street are two different jobs.

th-1026-2.text:
Hard sparring or ten rounds on the pads: which leaves you more sore?

And which one made you better?

th-1026-3.text:
Three minutes of arm circles isn't a warm up.

Skip rope until you sweat, then shadowbox at half speed for two rounds. Your first hard breath shouldn't come in your first real round.

th-1027-1.text:
Try the new move in sparring. Even if you lose the round.

Winning with your best three tricks teaches you nothing. Failing with a new one shows you what to fix.

th-1027-2.text:
Music in the gym or no music?

Some people can't think with it. Some can't start without it. Which one are you?

th-1027-3.text:
My first Muay Thai fight was a draw.

I hit him with a right hand while the ref was separating us. He went down. It was not clean at all.

Official result: a draw. The scorecard doesn't care what you remember.

th-1028-1.text:
Rest isn't lazy.

Skipping it is how you end up with a six week injury. Sleep, eat real food, take the day off. The boring half of training is the half that holds the rest together.

th-1028-2.text:
Boxing or Muay Thai for a total beginner?

Skip "whichever your gym teaches". Pick one and give me the reason.

th-1028-3.text:
Stuck on a plateau? Change the rule, not the effort.

Spar a round using only your jab. Or fight a round going backward. You'll find the gaps your usual game hides.

th-1029-1.text:
Being scared of getting hit doesn't make you a bad fighter.

It makes you honest. The ones who claim they don't care usually haven't been hit properly yet.

th-1029-2.text:
How long until you stopped closing your eyes when something came at your face?

First week, first month, or still working on it?

th-1029-3.text:
Training in the morning? A banana and a glass of water is enough.

Skip the big breakfast you can't hold down in round three. Eat the real meal after.
